Paul's journey toward Jerusalem (verses 1–7)

When our affairs go well, we ought to recognize God's Providence.

Whenever Paul arrived somewhere, he searched for disciples and found them.

His friends foresaw his troubles. Because they loved him and cared about the church, they mistakenly thought God's honor would be better served if he remained free.

Their earnest efforts to dissuade him made his godly determination even clearer.

Paul teaches us by both instruction and example to pray continually.

The disciples' last farewell was made sweeter by prayer.

Agabus predicts trouble; Paul reaches Jerusalem (verses 8–18)

Paul received clear warning of the suffering ahead, so it would neither surprise nor terrify him.

Scripture gives us the same warning: through many troubles we must enter God's kingdom.

His friends' weeping began to weaken his resolution. Yet Christ had told his followers to take up their cross.

Paul was distressed that they so insistently pressed him toward something he could not do without wronging his conscience.

When trouble approaches, we should not merely say, “The Lord's will must be done; there is nothing we can do.”

Rather we should say, “Let the Lord's will be done.” His will expresses divine wisdom, and he orders all things according to it.

Once trouble comes, God's accomplished will should quiet our grief.

When trouble approaches, God's promised will should quiet our fears.

Our response ought to be Amen; let it happen.

It is an honor to become an old disciple of Christ, kept by God's grace in the path of duty, steady in faith, growing in experience into old age.

We should welcome fellowship with such believers, because their years can teach us wisdom.

Many believers in Jerusalem received Paul gladly.

We may imagine that we too would have welcomed him, but unless we welcome his doctrine, we would not truly welcome the apostle.

Paul joins ceremonial observances (verses 19–26)

Paul credited God with all his success, and the Jerusalem believers gave God praise.

God had honored him greatly, yet the other apostles did not envy his fruitful service; they glorified the Lord.

James and the elders asked Paul to accommodate Jewish Christians through some compliance with ceremonial law.

They thought this was prudent.

But Henry judges that clinging to ceremonial shadows after their substance, Christ, had come was a serious weakness.

The religion Paul preached did not destroy the law but fulfilled it. He proclaimed Christ as the law's goal for righteousness, along with repentance and faith, in which the law retains its proper use.

Even disciples of Christ sometimes gave too little regard to Paul, despite his remarkable character and work, simply because his attachment to Jewish ceremonies differed from theirs.

This illustrates the danger of religious prejudice.

The apostles were not beyond criticism in every action.

Henry adds that it would be difficult to defend Paul from the charge of yielding too much in this matter.

Trying to win the approval of unyielding zealots and party-minded people is usually futile.

Paul's concession did not succeed: the very action intended to calm opposition inflamed it.

But God overruled both the elders' advice and Paul's compliance for a wiser purpose.

Nothing would satisfy people determined to destroy Christianity.

Sincere integrity is safer than compliance against one's better judgment.

This also warns us never to pressure people to act contrary to their conscientious convictions merely to please us.

The Romans rescue Paul from his accusers (verses 27–40)

Paul was attacked in the temple, where he ought to have been safe.

His opponents falsely accused him of teaching and acting against Mosaic ordinances.

People who intend well and act lawfully often find themselves accused of actions they never contemplated.

Sometimes an attempt to oblige others becomes the very thing used against us.

God may protect his servants through people who have no affection for Christianity but who feel compassion for suffering people or value public peace.

Many are misled by false ideas about good people and faithful ministers.

Yet the Lord intervenes at the right time to protect his servants from wicked and unreasonable people, giving them opportunities to speak for themselves, plead the Redeemer's cause and spread his glorious gospel.

Paul at Cesarea. The prophecy of Agabus, Paul at Jerusalem. | (8-18) |
He is persuaded to join in ceremonial observances. | (19-26) |
Being in danger from the Jews, he is rescued by the Romans. | (27-40) |
Verses 1-7
Providence must be acknowledged when our affairs go on well. Wherever Paul came, he inquired what disciples were there, and found them out. Foreseeing his troubles, from love to him, and concern for the church, they wrongly thought it would be most for the glory of God that he should continue at liberty; but their earnestness to dissuade him from it, renders his pious resolution the more illustrious. He has taught us by example, as well as by rule, to pray always, to pray without ceasing. Their last farewell was sweetened with prayer.
[Acts.21.8-Acts.21.18]
Verses 8-18
Paul had express warning of his troubles, that when they came, they might be no surprise or terror to him. The general notice given us, that through much tribulation we must enter into the kingdom of God, should be of the same use to us. Their weeping began to weaken and slacken his resolution Has not our Master told us to take up our cross? It was a trouble to him, that they should so earnestly press him to do that in which he could not gratify them without wronging his conscience. When we see trouble coming, it becomes us to say, not only, The will of the Lord must be done, and there is no remedy; but, Let the will of the Lord be done; for his will is his wisdom, and he doeth all according to the counsel of it. When a trouble is come, this must allay our griefs, that the will of the Lord is done; when we see it coming, this must silence our fears, that the will of the Lord shall be done; and we ought to say, Amen, let it be done. It is honourable to be an old disciple of Jesus Christ, to have been enabled by the grace of God to continue long in a course of duty, stedfast in the faith, growing more and more experienced, to a good old age. And with these old disciples one would choose to lodge; for the multitude of their years shall teach wisdom. Many brethren at Jerusalem received Paul gladly. We think, perhaps, that if we had him among us, we should gladly receive him; but we should not, if, having his doctrine, we do not gladly receive that.
[Acts.21.19-Acts.21.26]
Verses 19-26
Paul ascribed all his success to God, and to God they gave the praise. God had honoured him more than any of the apostles, yet they did not envy him; but on the contrary, glorified the Lord. They could not do more to encourage Paul to go on cheerfully in his work. James and the elders of the church at Jerusalem, asked Paul to gratify the believing Jews, by some compliance with the ceremonial law. They thought it was prudent in him to conform thus far. It was great weakness to be so fond of the shadows, when the substance was come. The religion Paul preached, tended not to destroy the law, but to fulfil it. He preached Christ, the end of the law for righteousness, and repentance and faith, in which we are to make great use of the law. The weakness and evil of the human heart strongly appear, when we consider how many, even of the disciples of Christ, had not due regard to the most eminent minister that even lived. Not the excellence of his character, nor the success with which God blessed his labours, could gain their esteem and affection, seeing that he did not render the same respect as themselves to mere ceremonial observances. How watchful should we be against prejudices! The apostles were not free from blame in all they did; and it would be hard to defend Paul from the charge of giving way too much in this matter. It is vain to attempt to court the favour of zealots, or bigots to a party. This compliance of Paul did not answer, for the very thing by which he hoped to pacify the Jews, provoked them, and brought him into trouble. But the all-wise God overruled both their advice and Paul's compliance with it, to serve a better purpose than was intended. It was in vain to think of pleasing men who would be pleased with nothing but the rooting out of Christianity. Integrity and uprightness will be more likely to preserve us than insincere compliances. And it should warn us not to press men to doing what is contrary to their own judgment to oblige us.
[Acts.21.27-Acts.21.40]
Verses 27-40
In the temple, where Paul should have been protected as in a place of safety, he was violently set upon. They falsely charged him with ill doctrine and ill practice against the Mosaic ceremonies. It is no new thing for those who mean honestly and act regularly, to have things laid to their charge which they know not and never thought of. It is common for the wise and good to have that charged against them by malicious people, with which they thought to have obliged them. God often makes those a protection to his people, who have no affection to them, but only have compassion for sufferers, and regard to the public peace. And here see what false, mistaken notions of good people and good ministers, many run away with. But God seasonably interposes for the safety of his servants, from wicked and unreasonable men; and gives them opportunities to speak for themselves, to plead for the Redeemer, and to spread abroad his glorious gospel.

Paul describes his conversion (verses 1–11)

Paul addressed the enraged crowd with the customary courtesy and goodwill.

He described his earlier life carefully and made clear that his conversion was entirely the work of God.

Condemned sinners are struck blind by the power of darkness, and that blindness continues, as it did among those who rejected the gospel.

But sinners brought under conviction are temporarily blinded not by darkness but by light, as Paul was.

For a time they are bewildered and uncertain so that afterward they may receive spiritual understanding.

A straightforward account of how the Lord brought us from opposing the gospel to professing and promoting it, told in the right spirit, can move hearers more deeply than elaborate speeches.

Such an account does not itself prove every Christian truth, but the transformation in Paul's life provided striking confirmation of God's power.

Paul is sent to the Gentiles (verses 12–21)

Paul went on to describe how his change of life was confirmed.

When the Lord chooses a sinner to know his will, he humbles and enlightens that person and leads them to Christ and his blessed gospel.

Jesus is called the Righteous One, for he is Jesus Christ the righteous.

Everyone called to understand God's will must look to Christ, through whom God has revealed his goodwill toward us.

The great gospel privilege signified and sealed by baptism is the forgiveness of sins.

When Paul was commanded to be baptized and wash away his sins, he was called to receive the comfort of pardon through Jesus Christ, take hold of Christ's righteousness and seek power to put his sinful desires to death.

Do not stop at the outward sign. Make sure you possess the cleansing from sin that it signifies.

The gospel duty to which baptism commits us is to seek forgiveness in Christ's name and in dependence upon him and his righteousness.

God appoints his workers both their time and their place.

They ought to follow his direction even when it contradicts their preferences.

Providence plans more wisely for us than we plan for ourselves.

When Christ sends someone, his Spirit accompanies that servant and enables them to see fruit from their labors.

Yet no one is reconciled to the gospel except through God's special grace.

Paul appeals to his Roman citizenship (verses 22–30)

The crowd listened to Paul's account of his conversion until he mentioned his mission to the Gentiles.

Their national prejudices were so strong that they refused to hear more.

Their violent behavior astonished the Roman commander, who assumed that Paul must have committed a terrible crime.

Paul invoked his rights as a Roman citizen, exempting him from coercive examinations and punishments intended to force a confession.

His manner showed remarkable peace and confidence.

The commander was surprised that a Jew living in modest circumstances possessed such a valuable privilege; the commander had paid a great deal for his own citizenship.

Paul replied that he had been born with it.

Let us place far greater value on the freedom into which God's children are born, a liberty no amount of money can purchase for someone who remains unregenerate.

Paul's appeal immediately stopped the unlawful treatment.

Many people avoid sinful actions because they fear human authorities, although they would not be restrained by reverence for God.

Paul simply asked, “Is it lawful?”

He knew God could sustain him through any suffering genuinely required for Christ's sake.

But if the threatened suffering was unlawful and could properly be avoided, his faith directed him to avoid it.

He never turned away from the cross his divine Master placed along his path; neither did he leave that path in search of an unnecessary cross.

Verses 1-11
The apostle addressed the enraged multitude, in the customary style of respect and good-will. Paul relates the history of his early life very particularly; he notices that his conversion was wholly the act of God. Condemned sinners are struck blind by the power of darkness, and it is a lasting blindness, like that of the unbelieving Jews. Convinced sinners are struck blind as Paul was, not by darkness, but by light. They are for a time brought to be at a loss within themselves, but it is in order to their being enlightened. A simple relation of the Lord's dealings with us, in bringing us, from opposing, to profess and promote his gospel, when delivered in a right spirit and manner, will sometimes make more impression that laboured speeches, even though it amounts not to the full proof of the truth, such as was shown in the change wrought in the apostle.
[Acts.22.12-Acts.22.21]
Verses 12-21
The apostle goes on to relate how he was confirmed in the change he had made. The Lord having chosen the sinner, that he should know his will, he is humbled, enlightened, and brought to the knowledge of Christ and his blessed gospel. Christ is here called that Just One; for he is Jesus Christ the righteous. Those whom God has chosen to know his will, must look to Jesus, for by him God has made known his good-will to us. The great gospel privilege, sealed to us by baptism, is the pardon of sins. Be baptized, and wash away thy sins; that is, receive the comfort of the pardon of thy sins in and through Jesus Christ, and lay hold on his righteousness for that purpose; and receive power against sin, for the mortifying of thy corruptions. Be baptized, and rest not in the sign, but make sure of the thing signified, the putting away of the filth of sin. The great gospel duty, to which by our baptism we are bound, is, to seek for the pardon of our sins in Christ's name, and in dependence on him and his righteousness. God appoints his labourers their day and their place, and it is fit they should follow his appointment, though it may cross their own will. Providence contrives better for us than we do for ourselves; we must refer ourselves to God's guidance. If Christ send any one, his Spirit shall go along with him, and give him to see the fruit of his labours. But nothing can reconcile man's heart to the gospel, except the special grace of God.
[Acts.22.22-Acts.22.30]
Verses 22-30
The Jews listened to Paul's account of his conversion, but the mention of his being sent to the Gentiles, was so contrary to all their national prejudices, that they would hear no more. Their frantic conduct astonished the Roman officer, who supposed that Paul must have committed some great crime. Paul pleaded his privilege as a Roman citizen, by which he was exempted from all trials and punishments which might force him to confess himself guilty. The manner of his speaking plainly shows what holy security and serenity of mind he enjoyed. As Paul was a Jew, in low circumstances, the Roman officer questioned how he obtained so valuable a distinction; but the apostle told him he was free born. Let us value that freedom to which all the children of God are born; which no sum of money, however large, can purchase for those who remain unregenerate. This at once put a stop to his trouble. Thus many are kept from evil practices by the fear of man, who would not be held back from them by the fear of God. The apostle asks, simply, Is it lawful? He knew that the God whom he served would support him under all sufferings for his name's sake. But if it were not lawful, the apostle's religion directed him, if possible, to avoid it. He never shrunk from a cross which his Divine Master laid upon his onward road; and he never stept aside out of that road to take one up.

Paul defends himself before the council (verses 1–5)

Here we see what an honest person is like.

Such a person sets God continually before them and lives as in his sight.

Their conscience governs their words and deeds. According to the best of their knowledge, they avoid evil and cling to what is good.

They act conscientiously in every part of life.

People who live this way before God can, like Paul, have confidence both toward God and toward others.

Paul's answer to the high priest included a deserved rebuke and a warning of judgment.

Nevertheless, Henry judges that Paul seems to have spoken with too much anger after being struck.

Even people occupying high office may be told about their failures and may rightly face public complaint.

But these objections must be expressed appropriately, because God's law still requires respect for those in authority.

The council divides; Christ reassures Paul (verses 6–11)

The Pharisees held the traditional Jewish belief in resurrection.

The Sadducees rejected Scripture and divine revelation in this matter. They denied a future state, and therefore had neither hope of everlasting joy nor fear of everlasting suffering.

Paul could truthfully say that he was being tried because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead.

It was legitimate for him to state his position on this disputed question and thereby move Pharisees to protect him from unlawful violence.

How easily God can defend his cause!

The Jewish leaders appeared united in opposition to Christianity, but their motives differed.

The wicked have no secure friendship with one another.

God can turn their apparent agreement into open disagreement in an instant.

The Roman commander rescued Paul from violent people, but could not tell him what the future held.

God's own consolation was much more valuable.

Whoever opposes us, we need not fear if the Lord stands beside us.

Christ desires his faithful servants to remain joyful and courageous.

Paul may have thought that he would never reach Rome.

But God assured him that he would testify there too, because Paul's desire to go to Rome arose from a wish to honor Christ and do good.

A conspiracy is exposed; Paul is sent to Caesarea (verses 12–24)

False religious beliefs, when adopted by people governed by sinful passions, can provoke astonishing cruelty.

Yet God easily defeats the most carefully designed schemes of wickedness.

Paul understood that divine Providence ordinarily works through reasonable and prudent means.

Had he neglected the means available to protect himself, he could not have rightly expected God to preserve him by extraordinary intervention.

A person unwilling to use available abilities and opportunities has neither reason nor revelation guaranteeing God's assistance.

By trusting the Lord, we may expect him to preserve us from every evil work and bring us safely into his heavenly kingdom.

Heavenly Father, through your Holy Spirit and for Christ's sake, grant us this precious faith.

Lysias writes to Felix (verses 25–35)

God has instruments for every task he intends to accomplish.

The natural abilities and moral virtues of unbelieving people have often been used to protect his persecuted servants.

Even people who care little about Christian doctrine may recognize the difference between the honest conduct of upright believers and the zeal of false religious professors.

All human hearts are in God's hand.

Blessed are those who trust him and commit their way to him.

Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
Paul's defence before the council of the Jews. | (1-5) |
Paul's defence. He receives a Divine assurance that he shall go to Rome. | (6-11) |
The Jews conspire to kill Paul, Lysias sends him to Cesarea. | (12-24) |

Verses 1-5
See here the character of an honest man. He sets God before him, and lives as in his sight. He makes conscience of what he says and does, and, according to the best of his knowledge, he keeps from whatever is evil, and cleaves to what is good. He is conscientious in all his words and conduct. Those who thus live before God, may, like Paul, have confidence both toward God and man. Though the answer of Paul contained a just rebuke and prediction, he seems to have been too angry at the treatment he received in uttering them. Great men may be told of their faults, and public complaints may be made in a proper manner; but the law of God requires respect for those in authority.
[Acts.23.6-Acts.23.11]
Verses 6-11
The Pharisees were correct in the faith of the Jewish church. The Sadducees were no friends to the Scripture or Divine revelation; they denied a future state; they had neither hope of eternal happiness, nor dread of eternal misery. When called in question for his being a Christian, Paul might truly say he was called in question for the hope of the resurrection of the dead. It was justifiable in him, by this profession of his opinion on that disputed point, to draw off the Pharisees from persecuting him, and to lead them to protect him from this unlawful violence. How easily can God defend his own cause! Though the Jews seemed to be perfectly agreed in their conspiracy against religion, yet they were influenced by very different motives. There is no true friendship among the wicked, and in a moment, and with the utmost ease, God can turn their union into open enmity. Divine consolations stood Paul in the most stead; the chief captain rescued him out of the hands of cruel men, but the event he could not tell. Whoever is against us, we need not fear, if the Lord stand by us. It is the will of Christ, that his servants who are faithful, should be always cheerful. He might think he should never see Rome; but God tells him, even in that he should be gratified, since he desired to go there only for the honour of Christ, and to do good.
[Acts.23.12-Acts.23.24]
Verses 12-24
False religious principles, adopted by carnal men, urge on to such wickedness, as human nature would hardly be supposed capable of. Yet the Lord readily disappoints the best concerted schemes of iniquity. Paul knew that the Divine providence acts by reasonable and prudent means; and that, if he neglected to use the means in his power, he could not expect God's providence to work on his behalf. He who will not help himself according to his means and power, has neither reason nor revelation to assure him that he shall receive help from God. Believing in the Lord, we and ours shall be kept from every evil work, and kept to his kingdom. Heavenly Father, give us by thy Holy Spirit, for Christ's sake, this precious faith.
[Acts.23.25-Acts.23.35]
Verses 25-35
God has instruments for every work. The natural abilities and moral virtues of the heathens often have been employed to protect his persecuted servants. Even the men of the world can discern between the conscientious conduct of upright believers, and the zeal of false professors, though they disregard or understand not their doctrinal principles. All hearts are in God's hand, and those are blessed who put their trust in him, and commit their ways unto him.

Tertullus accuses Paul (verses 1–9)

Here we see a danger faced by powerful people: their accomplishments are praised beyond measure while their sins are never honestly exposed.

Such flattery hardens people and encourages them to continue doing evil, as happened with Felix.

God's prophets were accused of disturbing the land, and the Lord Jesus himself was accused of misleading the nation.

The same accusations were now brought against Paul.

Selfish passions often drive people to persecute others.

Skills of speech and public persuasion can be used to mislead people and turn them against the truth.

How different Paul and Felix will appear on the day of judgment from the descriptions Tertullus offered!

Christians should neither seek the praise of irreligious people nor be troubled by their insults.

Worldly flatterers can make the most wicked people appear almost divine, while treating the best people on earth as dangerous rebels.

Paul answers Felix (verses 10–21)

Paul gave a truthful explanation of his conduct.

It cleared him of criminal charges and exposed the real reason for the violence directed against him.

We must never abandon a good path simply because others give it a bad name.

When we worship God, it is a comfort to worship the God of our fathers, receiving no other rule for faith and conduct than the Scriptures.

Scripture also teaches that there will be a resurrection followed by final judgment.

The prophets and their teaching were to be tested by their fruit.

Paul labored to maintain a conscience without offense toward both God and human beings.

He diligently avoided sin and pursued godliness in every situation.

What if other people accuse us of loving God too much?

Do we shrink from that accusation?

Many people would rather be accused of almost any weakness—even serious wrongdoing—than of earnest love for Jesus Christ and devotion to his service.

Can such people really expect Christ to acknowledge them when he comes in glory before God's angels?

What would please the Savior more than seeing a faithful servant on earth gladly admit, if it is considered an offense, that he loves the Lord who died for him with all his heart, soul, mind and strength?

Such a believer will not silently watch God's word despised or hear his name profaned.

He will rather risk the world's ridicule and hatred than incur the disapproval of the gracious Lord whose love is better than life.

Felix trembles but postpones repentance (verses 22–27)

Paul reasoned with Felix about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come.

These were exactly the subjects the oppressive governor and the woman living with him needed to hear.

They needed repentance, forgiveness and the grace of the gospel.

Righteousness concerns our conduct in life, particularly toward other people.

Self-control concerns the ordering and government of our inner life before God.

Someone who neglects both has neither the true form nor the power of godliness and faces God's righteous anger at judgment.

The prospect of future judgment can make even the boldest person tremble.

Felix trembled—but nothing more followed.

Many hear God's word and become frightened without being changed.

They fear sin's consequences yet continue loving and practicing it.

Delay is dangerous whenever eternal salvation is at stake.

Felix deferred the conversation until a more convenient moment.

Scripture does not report that such a moment ever came.

Now is the accepted time; today is the day of salvation.

Felix eagerly ended the interview, but what business could be more urgent than reforming his life or saving his soul?

Many sinners start up like someone awakened by a sudden loud noise, then fall almost immediately back into sleep.

We must not be deceived by occasional outward displays of religious interest, whether in ourselves or others.

Above all, we must not treat God's word lightly.

Do we imagine that hearts naturally become softer with age, or that the world's influence inevitably weakens?

We are in danger now, and tomorrow may be too late.

[Acts.24.1-Acts.24.9]
Chapter 24
Chapter Outline
The speech of Tertullus against Paul. | (1-9) |
Paul's defence before Felix. | (10-21) |
Felix trembles at the reasoning of Paul. | (22-27) |
Verses 1-9
See here the unhappiness of great men, and a great unhappiness it is, to have their services praised beyond measure, and never to be faithfully told of their faults; hereby they are hardened and encouraged in evil, like Felix. God's prophets were charged with being troublers of the land, and our Lord Jesus Christ, that he perverted the nation; the very same charges were brought against Paul. The selfish and evil passions of men urge them forward, and the graces and power of speech, too often have been used to mislead and prejudice men against the truth. How different will the characters of Paul and Felix appear at the day of judgement, from what they are represented in the speech of Tertullus! Let not Christians value the applause, or be troubled at the revilings of ungodly men, who represent the vilest of the human race almost as gods, and the excellent of the earth as pestilences and movers of sedition.
[Acts.24.10-Acts.24.21]
Verses 10-21
Paul gives a just account of himself, which clears him from crime, and likewise shows the true reason of the violence against him. Let us never be driven from any good way by its having an ill name. It is very comfortable, in worshipping God, to look to him as the God of our fathers, and to set up no other rule of faith or practice but the Scriptures. This shows there will be a resurrection to a final judgment. Prophets and their doctrines were to be tried by their fruits. Paul's aim was to have a conscience void of offence. His care and endeavour was to abstain from many things, and to abound in the exercises of religion at all times; both towards God. and towards man. If blamed for being more earnest in the things of God than our neighbours, what is our reply? Do we shrink from the accusation? How many in the world would rather be accused of any weakness, nay, even of wickedness, than of an earnest, fervent feeling of love to the Lord Jesus Christ, and of devotedness to his service! Can such think that He will confess them when he comes in his glory, and before the angels of God? If there is any sight pleasing to the God of our salvation, and a sight at which the angels rejoice, it is, to behold a devoted follower of the Lord, here upon earth, acknowledging that he is guilty, if it be a crime, of loving the Lord who died for him, with all his heart, and soul, and mind, and strength. And that he will not in silence see God's word despised, or hear his name profaned; he will rather risk the ridicule and the hatred of the world, than one frown from that gracious Being whose love is better than life.
[Acts.24.22-Acts.24.27]
Verses 22-27
The apostle reasoned concerning the nature and obligations of righteousness, temperance, and of a judgment to come; thus showing the oppressive judge and his profligate mistress, their need of repentance, forgiveness, and of the grace of the gospel. Justice respects our conduct in life, particularly in reference to others; temperance, the state and government of our souls, in reference to God. He who does not exercise himself in these, has neither the form nor the power of godliness, and must be overwhelmed with the Divine wrath in the day of God's appearing. A prospect of the judgment to come, is enough to make the stoutest heart to tremble. Felix trembled, but that was all. Many are startled by the word of God, who are not changed by it. Many fear the consequences of sin, yet continue in the love and practice of sin. In the affairs of our souls, delays are dangerous. Felix put off this matter to a more convenient season, but we do not find that the more convenient season ever came. Behold now is the accepted time; hear the voice of the Lord to-day. He was in haste to turn from hearing the truth. Was any business more urgent than for him to reform his conduct, or more important than the salvation of his soul! Sinners often start up like a man roused from his sleep by a loud noise, but soon sink again into their usual drowsiness. Be not deceived by occasional appearances of religion in ourselves or in others. Above all, let us not trifle with the word of God. Do we expect that as we advance in life our hearts will grow softer, or that the influence of the world will decline? Are we not at this moment in danger of being lost for ever? Now is the day of salvation; tomorrow may be too late.

See how restless malicious people are.

Persecutors treat the opportunity to satisfy their hatred as a special favor.

But preaching Christ as the fulfillment and goal of the law was no offense against that law.

In times of persecution, God's people need wisdom and prudence as well as patience.

Innocent people may rightly insist on their innocence.

Paul was prepared to submit to lawful proceedings and let the legal process take its course.

If he truly deserved death, he would accept the penalty.

But if the accusations were false, no one could justly deliver him to his enemies.

For the moment Paul was neither released nor condemned.

This shows how gradually Providence sometimes unfolds.

We often discover that both our hopes and our fears were premature, as God keeps us waiting on him.

Festus consults Agrippa about Paul (verses 13–27)

Agrippa governed Galilee.

Festus acknowledged an important Roman legal principle: a person accused of wrongdoing must have the opportunity to confront the accusers and answer the charges (verse 16).

How many hasty and unjust judgments does that principle condemn!

Even a non-Christian governor, guided only by natural understanding, could follow the law and established custom in this matter.

Yet many professing Christians neglect truth, justice and charity when judging brothers and sisters.

Worldly people and political officials may regard questions of divine worship, salvation and the gospel as doubtful or unimportant.

Notice how lightly Festus spoke of Christ and the controversy between Jewish leaders and Christians.

But the day is approaching when Festus and everyone else will recognize that the affairs of the entire Roman Empire were insignificant compared with the truth of Christ's resurrection.

Those who had the means to learn God's truth yet despised them will understand their folly and sin.

A distinguished company gathered to hear Paul.

They intended only to satisfy their curiosity about a prisoner, but they were about to hear the gospel.

People still sometimes come to hear God's word with great pomp, motivated by curiosity rather than a desire for truth.

Although ministers today do not ordinarily stand in the dock defending their lives, some hearers still sit in judgment upon them, looking for any statement they can use as a charge rather than listening to learn God's will for their salvation.

Yet all the grandeur of the assembly was eclipsed by the real glory of the poor prisoner.

What were their splendid clothes and rank beside Paul's wisdom, grace, holiness, courage and steadfast endurance for Christ?

It is a great mercy when God makes our innocence and upright conduct plain, leaving opponents without any proven charge.

Sometimes he causes even our enemies to do us justice.

Paul defends himself before Agrippa (verses 1–11)

Christianity teaches us to explain the reason for our hope, while also giving proper honor to those entitled to it—without flattery or fear of human beings.

Agrippa knew the Old Testament well and was therefore better equipped to judge the dispute about whether Jesus was the Messiah.

Surely ministers preaching faith in Christ may expect to receive a patient hearing.

Paul affirmed that he retained everything good in the religious training he had received.

He had lived morally and avoided the public wickedness and cunning greed of some Pharisees.

He had also held sound religious beliefs and revered God's ancient promise to the fathers, making that promise the foundation of his hope.

Paul understood that none of this former morality could justify him before God.

Yet he mentioned it because it disproved his enemies' charges and could bring honor to Christ.

Though he counted these things as loss in order to gain Christ, they were relevant to his defense.

His Christian faith did not continue his youthful zeal for the ceremonial law.

The sacrifices and offerings had been fulfilled and superseded by the great Sacrifice they foreshadowed.

He no longer treated the ceremonial washings as binding, because Christ's priesthood had fulfilled the Levitical priesthood.

But the great principles of true religion remained those for which he had always cared.

Christ and heaven are two central doctrines of the gospel.

God has given eternal life, and that life is in his Son.

These were the matters promised to the fathers.

Israel's continual religious duties testified to faith in that promise.

The prospect of eternal life should move us to steadfast devotion.

The Sadducees opposed Paul for teaching resurrection; other Jewish leaders joined them because he proclaimed Jesus as risen and as Israel's promised Redeemer.

Many divine promises seem impossible only because people forget the infinite power and perfection of the God who promised them.

Paul acknowledged that during his days as a Pharisee, he had been a bitter enemy of Christianity.

Everything in his background seemed opposed to conversion.

Even people who were outwardly strict before conversion may later find much to repent of, including actions they previously regarded as religious duties.

Paul recounts his conversion and mission (verses 12–23)

Paul became a Christian through God's power, when Christ revealed himself both to him and within him, even while Paul was actively pursuing sin.

He became a minister through Christ's authority, because the same Lord who appeared in heavenly glory commanded him to preach to Gentiles.

The world lies in darkness and must receive light.

People ignorant of the way to eternal peace must be taught it.

But the world also lies in sin and needs sanctification and reform.

It is not enough to open people's eyes; their hearts must be renewed.

They must be brought not only from darkness to light, but also from Satan's power to God.

Everyone genuinely turned from sin to God receives more than pardon: a rich eternal inheritance.

Forgiveness opens the way to that inheritance.

Nobody can be happy without holiness. Those who will be saints in heaven must begin to be saints while on earth.

We are made holy and saved through faith in Jesus Christ.

By faith we rely on him as the Lord our Righteousness and surrender ourselves to him as the Lord who rules us.

Through this faith we receive forgiveness, the gift of the Holy Spirit and eternal life.

Christ's cross offended the Jewish leaders.

They were enraged that Paul proclaimed the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies, including that Christ would be the first or principal one raised from the dead.

The prophets also foretold that the Messiah would bring Gentiles to know God.

What reasonable objection could anyone have to this?

A genuine convert can explain the reasons for Christian hope and the change in personal life.

Yet people who preach repentance and conversion have often suffered persecution for doing so.

Festus and Agrippa hear Paul's appeal (verses 24–32)

We should speak truthfully and soberly in every situation, without being unsettled by unjust criticism.

Faithful gospel workers are often dismissed as dreamers or mad people because they believe wonderful events and insist that others, regardless of social status, need the same faith and diligence for salvation.

The apostles, prophets and even the Son of God faced such accusations.

Those made wise for salvation by divine grace need not be shaken by them.

Agrippa saw much evidence in favor of Christianity.

For a time his reasoning and judgment were persuaded, but his heart was not changed.

His attitude and conduct remained far from the humility and spiritual character of the gospel.

Many people become almost persuaded to take faith seriously.

They recognize the excellence of God's ways and feel strong convictions about their duties, yet they fail to act on them.

Paul urged everyone to become truly Christian.

Christ's grace is sufficient for all, and faith in him is absolutely necessary for salvation.

The gospel offers deliverance from spiritual bondage to Gentiles and the lost world.

Yet people are often unwilling to admit they need a transforming work of grace in their own hearts.

Beware of hesitation that becomes fatal.

Being almost a Christian is very different from possessing the faith and life of a true believer.

Verses 1-11
Christianity teaches us to give a reason of the hope that is in us, and also to give honour to whom honour is due, without flattery or fear of man. Agrippa was well versed in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, therefore could the better judge as to the controversy about Jesus being the Messiah. Surely ministers may expect, when they preach the faith of Christ, to be heard patiently. Paul professes that he still kept to all the good in which he was first educated and trained up. See here what his religion was. He was a moralist, a man of virtue, and had not learned the arts of the crafty, covetous Pharisees; he was not chargeable with any open vice and profaneness. He was sound in the faith. He always had a holy regard for the ancient promise made of God unto the fathers, and built his hope upon it. The apostle knew very well that all this would not justify him before God, yet he knew it was for his reputation among the Jews, and an argument that he was not such a man as they represented him to be. Though he counted this but loss, that he might win Christ, yet he mentioned it when it might serve to honour Christ. See here what Paul's religion is; he has not such zeal for the ceremonial law as he had in his youth; the sacrifices and offerings appointed by that, are done away by the great Sacrifice which they typified. Of the ceremonial cleansings he makes no conscience, and thinks the Levitical priesthood is done away in the priesthood of Christ; but, as to the main principles of his religion, he is as zealous as ever. Christ and heaven, are the two great doctrines of the gospel; that God has given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. These are the matter of the promise made unto the fathers. The temple service, or continual course of religious duties, day and night, was kept up as the profession of faith in the promise of eternal life, and in expectation of it. The prospect of eternal life should engage us to be diligent and stedfast in all religious exercises. Yet the Sadducees hated Paul for preaching the resurrection; and the other Jews joined them, because he testified that Jesus was risen, and was the promised Redeemer of Israel. Many things are thought to be beyond belief, only because the infinite nature and perfections of Him that has revealed, performed, or promised them, are overlooked. Paul acknowledged, that while he continued a Pharisee, he was a bitter enemy to Christianity. This was his character and manner of life in the beginning of his time; and there was every thing to hinder his being a Christian. Those who have been most strict in their conduct before conversion, will afterwards see abundant reason for humbling themselves, even on account of things which they then thought ought to have been done.
[Acts.26.12-Acts.26.23]
Verses 12-23
Paul was made a Christian by Divine power; by a revelation of Christ both to him and in him; when in the full career of his sin. He was made a minister by Divine authority: the same Jesus who appeared to him in that glorious light, ordered him to preach the gospel to the Gentiles. A world that sits in darkness must be enlightened; those must be brought to know the things that belong to their everlasting peace, who are yet ignorant of them. A world that lies in wickedness must be sanctified and reformed; it is not enough for them to have their eyes opened, they must have their hearts renewed; not enough to be turned from darkness to light, but they must be turned from the power of Satan unto God. All who are turned from sin to God, are not only pardoned, but have a grant of a rich inheritance. The forgiveness of sins makes way for this. None can be happy who are not holy; and to be saints in heaven we must be first saints on earth. We are made holy, and saved by faith in Christ; by which we rely upon Christ as the Lord our Righteousness, and give up ourselves to him as the Lord our Ruler; by this we receive the remission of sins, the gift of the Holy Ghost, and eternal life. The cross of Christ was a stumbling-block to the Jews, and they were in a rage at Paul's preaching the fulfilling of the Old Testament predictions. Christ should be the first that should rise from the dead; the Head or principal One. Also, it was foretold by the prophets, that the Gentiles should be brought to the knowledge of God by the Messiah; and what in this could the Jews justly be displeased at? Thus the true convert can give a reason of his hope, and a good account of the change manifest in him. Yet for going about and calling on men thus to repent and to be converted, vast numbers have been blamed and persecuted.
[Acts.26.24-Acts.26.32]
Verses 24-32
It becomes us, on all occasions, to speak the words of truth and soberness, and then we need not be troubled at the unjust censures of men. Active and laborious followers of the gospel often have been despised as dreamers or madmen, for believing such doctrines and such wonderful facts; and for attesting that the same faith and diligence, and an experience like their own, are necessary to all men, whatever their rank, in order to their salvation. But apostles and prophets, and the Son of God himself, were exposed to this charge; and none need be moved thereby, when Divine grace has made them wise unto salvation. Agrippa saw a great deal of reason for Christianity. His understanding and judgment were for the time convinced, but his heart was not changed. And his conduct and temper were widely different from the humility and spirituality of the gospel. Many are almost persuaded to be religious, who are not quite persuaded; they are under strong convictions of their duty, and of the excellence of the ways of God, yet do not pursue their convictions. Paul urged that it was the concern of every one to become a true Christian; that there is grace enough in Christ for all. He expressed his full conviction of the truth of the gospel, the absolute necessity of faith in Christ in order to salvation. Such salvation from such bondage, the gospel of Christ offers to the Gentiles; to a lost world. Yet it is with much difficulty that any person can be persuaded he needs a work of grace on his heart, like that which was needful for the conversion of the Gentiles. Let us beware of fatal hesitation in our own conduct; and recollect how far the being almost persuaded to be a Christian, is from being altogether such a one as every true believer is.

God's counsel had determined that Paul should reach Rome before Festus decided to send him there.

The Lord had work for Paul to do in that city.

The account records the route they followed and the places where they landed.

God encourages those who suffer for him to trust his care, because he can move unexpected people to befriend them.

Sailors must make the best use of whatever wind they receive.

Even when circumstances are against us, we should keep making progress as well as we can.

Others, including genuine Christians, spend so much effort merely maintaining their spiritual condition that they hardly advance.

Anyone would choose to lose possessions rather than life.

Nothing gives a good person greater satisfaction than knowing they can be a blessing to others.

Paul comforted his companions with the comfort he had received from God.

When we meet people who honor Christ in unfamiliar places, we have reason to praise God.

Discussion alone cannot convince sinners unless God's grace opens their understanding.

Although we grieve for those rejecting salvation, we should rejoice that God sends his salvation to others who will receive it.

If we are among them, we should thank him for the grace that made us different.

Paul remained resolved to know and preach Jesus Christ and him crucified.

When Christians are distracted from their chief purpose, let them ask: What does this have to do with Jesus? Does it bring us nearer to him and help us walk in him?

Paul preached Christ, not himself, without being ashamed of the gospel.

He had only limited opportunities for service while imprisoned, but he did not complain.

The door opened to him was narrow, yet no one was permitted to close it.

God made that opportunity fruitful for many, so that believers appeared even in Nero's household (Philippians 4:22).

Paul's chains themselves promoted the gospel (Philippians 1:13).

Believers in Rome and Christians throughout the world have reason to thank God that Paul spent a mature period of his Christian life in captivity.

Henry considers it probable that, while imprisoned and perhaps chained to a soldier, Paul wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Hebrews.

This is Henry's historical interpretation, not a verified assertion about the disputed authorship of Hebrews.

These writings display great Christian love and spiritual experience.

Today's believers may possess less of Paul's sense of triumph and heavenly joy.

Yet everyone who follows the same Savior has the same certainty of final safety and peace.

May we live increasingly in the Savior's love and seek his glory in every deed.

Through his strength, may we overcome our enemies now.

And through his undeserved grace and mercy, may we share the company of those who sit with him on his throne, as he overcame and sat at the Father's right hand forever.
classic_reading:
[Acts.28.1-Acts.28.10]
Chapter 28
Chapter Outline
Paul kindly received at Melita. | (1-10) |
He arrives at Rome. | (11-16) |
His conference with the Jews. | (17-22) |
Paul preaches to the Jews, and abides at Rome a prisoner. | (23-31) |
Verses 1-10
God can make strangers to be friends; friends in distress. Those who are despised for homely manners, are often more friendly than the more polished; and the conduct of heathens, or persons called barbarians, condemns many in civilized nations, professing to be Christians. The people thought that Paul was a murderer, and that the viper was sent by Divine justice, to be the avenger of blood. They knew that there is a God who governs the world, so that things do not come to pass by chance, no, not the smallest event, but all by Divine direction; and that evil pursues sinners; that there are good works which God will reward, and wicked works which he will punish. Also, that murder is a dreadful crime, one which shall not long go unpunished. But they thought all wicked people were punished in this life. Though some are made examples in this world, to prove that there is a God and a Providence, yet many are left unpunished, to prove that there is a judgment to come. They also thought all who were remarkably afflicted in this life were wicked people. Divine revelation sets this matter in a true light. Good men often are greatly afflicted in this life, for the trial and increase of their faith and patience. Observe Paul's deliverance from the danger. And thus in the strength of the grace of Christ, believers shake off the temptations of Satan, with holy resolution. When we despise the censures and reproaches of men, and look upon them with holy contempt, having the testimony of our consciences for us, then, like Paul, we shake off the viper into the fire. It does us no harm, except we are kept by it from our duty. God hereby made Paul remarkable among these people, and so made way for the receiving of the gospel. The Lord raises up friends for his people in every place whither he leads them, and makes them blessings to those in affliction.
[Acts.28.11-Acts.28.16]
Verses 11-16
The common events of travelling are seldom worthy of being told; but the comfort of communion with the saints, and kindness shown by friends, deserve particular mention. The Christians at Rome were so far from being ashamed of Paul, or afraid of owning him, because he was a prisoner, that they were the more careful to show him respect. He had great comfort in this. And if our friends are kind to us, God puts it into their hearts, and we must give him the glory. When we see those even in strange places, who bear Christ's name, fear God, and serve him, we should lift up our hearts to heaven in thanksgiving. How many great men have made their entry into Rome, crowned and in triumph, who really were plagues to the world! But here a good man makes his entry into Rome, chained as a poor captive, who was a greater blessing to the world than any other merely a man. Is not this enough to put us for ever out of conceit with worldly favour? This may encourage God's prisoners, that he can give them favour in the eyes of those that carry them captives. When God does not soon deliver his people out of bondage, yet makes it easy to them, or them easy under it, they have reason to be thankful.
[Acts.28.17-Acts.28.22]
Verses 17-22
It was for the honour of Paul that those who examined his case, acquitted him. In his appeal he sought not to accuse his nation, but only to clear himself. True Christianity settles what is of common concern to all mankind, and is not built upon narrow opinions and private interests. It aims at no worldly benefit or advantage, but all its gains are spiritual and eternal. It is, and always has been, the lot of Christ's holy religion, to be every where spoken against. Look through every town and village where Christ is exalted as the only Saviour of mankind, and where the people are called to follow him in newness of life, and we see those who give themselves up to Christ, still called a sect, a party, and reproached. And this is the treatment they are sure to receive, so long as there shall continue an ungodly man upon earth.
[Acts.28.23-Acts.28.31]
Verses 23-31
Paul persuaded the Jews concerning Jesus. Some were wrought upon by the word, and others hardened; some received the light, and others shut their eyes against it. And the same has always been the effect of the gospel. Paul parted with them, observing that the Holy Ghost had well described their state. Let all that hear the gospel, and do not heed it, tremble at their doom; for who shall heal them, if God does not? The Jews had afterwards much reasoning among themselves. Many have great reasoning, who do not reason aright. They find fault with one another's opinions, yet will not yield to truth. Nor will men's reasoning among themselves convince them, without the grace of God to open their understandings. While we mourn on account of such despisers, we should rejoice that the salvation of God is sent to others, who will receive it; and if we are of that number, we should be thankful to Him who hath made us to differ. The apostle kept to his principle, to know and preach nothing but Christ and him crucified. Christians, when tempted from their main business, should bring themselves back with this question, What does this concern the Lord Jesus? What tendency has it to bring us to him, and to keep us walking in him? The apostle preached not himself, but Christ, and he was not ashamed of the gospel of Christ. Though Paul was placed in a very narrow opportunity for being useful, he was not disturbed in it. Though it was not a wide door that was opened to him, yet no man was suffered to shut it; and to many it was an effectual door, so that there were saints even in Nero's household, [Phil.4.22] Php 4:22. We learn also from [Phil.1.13] Php 1:13, how God overruled Paul's imprisonment for the furtherance of the gospel. And not the residents at Rome only, but all the church of Christ, to the present day, and in the most remote corner of the globe, have abundant reason to bless God, that during the most mature period of his Christian life and experience, he was detained a prisoner. It was from his prison, probably chained hand to hand to the soldier who kept him, that the apostle wrote the epistles to the Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Hebrews; epistles showing, perhaps more than any others, the Christian love with which his heart overflowed, and the Christian experience with which his soul was filled. The believer of the present time may have less of triumph, and less of heavenly joy, than the apostle, but every follower of the same Saviour, is equally sure of safety and peace at the last. Let us seek to live more and more in the love of the Saviour; to labour to glorify Him by every action of our lives; and we shall assuredly, by his strength, be among the number of those who now overcome our enemies; and by his free grace and mercy, be hereafter among the blessed company who shall sit with Him upon his throne, even as He also has overcome, and is sitting on his Father's throne, at God's right hand for evermore.
